To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the plantation belt and upcountry were distinct regions in terms of their economic development before the Civil War; (2) they were not distinct in terms of their development in the decades after the war; (3) the plantation belt was not a region of economic stagnation in the postwar period; and (4) freedpeople in the plantation belt were able to establish themselves as independent farmers, and they had a higher rate of land ownership than freedpeople in the upcountry.
the Civil War and emancipation did not cause the demise of the planter system in the Tennessee upcountry.

the planters of the Antebelium era were the most successful farmers during the Civil War and Reconstruction, that they were able to maintain their dominance of the agricultural economy into the 1880s, and that the freedmen did not make significant economic progress during the period 1865-80.
In summary, our research is concerned with

two broad themes: first, the economic and social impact of the war and emancipation upon the plantation belt and the upcountry, and secondly, the extent to which these two regions were economically and socially similar or dissimilar in the prewar and immediate postwar eras.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the war was a major cause of the agricultural transformation that took place in Tennessee between 1860 and 1880, and that it was a cause that was felt most keenly in the Upcountry and the plantation belt.
the Civil War was a disaster for the white farmers of Tennessee, but that the freedmen and the black farmers of Tennessee benefited from the war.
the war and the Reconstruction era were not a time of agricultural progress and prosperity for Tennessee farmers, whether white or black.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Civil War and its immediate aftermath were a period of great change and uncertainty for white and black farmers in Tennessee.
the Civil War and Reconstruction had a profound impact upon the structure of Tennessee agriculture.
we have shown that the Civil War was not a'revolution' in the lives of white farmers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Civil War and emancipation were not the only factors shaping the course of the postbellum South.
the post-Civil War period in Tennessee saw the emergence of a new class of white farmers.
the South was more diverse than we had previously thought.
